record.title: Google releases PARDIG global precipitation datasets with author-reported multi-network evaluation
record.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Research released PARDIG, an experimental global precipitation-estimation dataset trained on sparse NASA/JAXA GPM spaceborne radar retrievals with satellite imagery and atmospheric-field inputs. It provides 0.1° grids every 15 minutes: a near-real-time stream for 2016 onward with roughly 2–8 hours effective latency, and a historical variant from 1999–2023. The paper reports better precipitation-detection scores than several global products across three regional radar networks and 36,678 quality-controlled stations, but these results have not been independently reproduced here. The product is openly licensed under CC BY 4.0 and explicitly is not an official warning product.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Google DeepMind and Google Research announced and documented two publicly accessible experimental PARDIG precipitation datasets: PARDIG-NRT for 2016 onward and PARDIG-LR for 1999–2023, at 0.1° spatial and 15-minute temporal resolution. Google documents CC BY 4.0 licensing and describes the near-real-time stream as updating in six-hour batches with approximately 2–8 hours effective latency.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper authors report that PARDIG-NRT scores above IMERG V07, MSWEP V3, ERA5 and HRES across analyzed precipitation thresholds and regions, using radar composites over the contiguous United States, Europe and Japan and 36,678 quality-controlled surface stations. The authors report their largest relative gains at heavier precipitation rates; the research desk has not independently recomputed these comparisons.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that a WeatherNext 3 precipitation head trained on an earlier but closely similar PARDIG version improved forecast scores against independent radar observations relative to the model’s IMERG-trained head; at a six-hour example, reported CRPS was approximately 15% lower. This is a paper-reported comparison, not an independently reproduced forecast result.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Google labels PARDIG experimental and says it is not intended, validated or approved for real-world warnings. The paper also reports weaker orographic performance at some high-elevation sites, an Alpine seasonal bias, and unconstrained extrapolation at polar latitudes.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The sources do not establish independent performance across all regions and regimes, including polar precipitation, complex mountain terrain, or operational warning use. The 1999–2007 historical variant also has a reported distribution shift associated with sparser early satellite observations.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent team has reproduced the paper’s cross-product comparisons using the released PARDIG data and evaluation protocol in this activation.
Transfer to polar latitudes, complex mountain terrain, sparsely gauged regions and consequential extreme events is not established by the reported evaluation.
The paper reports a distribution shift in PARDIG-LR prior to 2008; continuity with the later NRT record is not established for that early period.

brief.importance_rationale: If its reported skill and temporal coverage hold across independent evaluation, an openly available global precipitation record with 15-minute cadence could materially improve Earth-system research and downstream weather/hydrology workflows. This potential consequence does not establish the paper’s performance claims or global transfer.
limitations: All headline model-performance and downstream forecast comparisons are paper-author-reported; the research desk did not independently recompute them.
Ground-based validation covers three regional radar networks and a filtered station set; it does not establish uniform skill at every global location.
The paper reports occasional station-level deficits at high elevations and underestimation of wintertime versus summertime precipitation in the European Alps.
Polar estimates rely on unconstrained extrapolation because GPM coverage ends near 68° north/south; use there requires particular caution.
The historical PARDIG-LR record has a distributional shift before 2008 associated with sparser early satellite observations.
The official catalog calls PARDIG experimental and not intended, validated or approved for real-world warnings.

relationships.summary: The WeatherNext 3 development predates the PARDIG public release and reports precipitation-head evaluations; the PARDIG paper says a closely similar earlier PARDIG version was used as a training target and reports improved early-lead precipitation forecasts. Both performance accounts remain first-party.

brief.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Research released PARDIG, an experimental global precipitation-estimation dataset trained on sparse NASA/JAXA GPM spaceborne radar retrievals with satellite imagery and atmospheric-field inputs. It provides 0.1° grids every 15 minutes: a near-real-time stream for 2016 onward with roughly 2–8 hours effective latency, and a historical variant from 1999–2023. The paper reports better precipitation-detection scores than several global products across three regional radar networks and 36,678 quality-controlled stations, but these results have not been independently reproduced here. The product is openly licensed under CC BY 4.0 and explicitly is not an official warning product.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report higher hourly precipitation Critical Success Index than IMERG V07, MSWEP V3, ERA5 and HRES across three regional radar composites and a filtered set of 36,678 station gauges. Reported tests cover main comparison periods 2016–2023, with held-out 2024–2025 radar checks in the United States and Japan. They also report a roughly 15% lower six-hour CRPS for the WeatherNext 3 head trained on an earlier PARDIG version versus its IMERG head.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public dataset and documentation are accessible under CC BY 4.0 without a separate access application. Google documents near-real-time batches approximately every six hours and effective latency varying around 2–8 hours. The research paper and product documentation were inspected; no data subset or benchmark was independently executed in this activation.
technical.mechanism: A spherical graph-mesh transformer is trained to predict sparse, high-precision GPM CORRA spaceborne radar retrievals from denser atmospheric analyses and multispectral satellite imagery. PARDIG-NRT uses ECMWF HRES plus SatWeave geostationary mosaics; PARDIG-LR uses ERA5, GridSat-B1 and passive-microwave satellite inputs. This sparse-to-dense estimate is delivered as global 0.1° precipitation grids every 15 minutes.
technical.regime: Global products; NRT begins in 2016 and updates in six-hour batches at roughly 2–8 hours effective latency, while PARDIG-LR covers 1999–2023. Native output spacing is 0.1° and 15 minutes. Radar/station evaluation coverage is limited to observational networks in the US, Europe and Japan and station locations; paper reports held-out radar evaluation to 2025 for the US and Japan. Product is experimental, not an official warning source.
technical.reproducibility: The paper, appendices and data documentation are publicly inspectable and data are CC BY 4.0. This activation did not download a data interval, reconstruct the score tables, or run an independent evaluation. Paper author-reported results remain unreproduced.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares against NASA IMERG Early/Final, MSWEP V3 gauge-corrected, ERA5 and ECMWF HRES using three regional radar products and station gauges. For the reported six-hour WeatherNext 3 example, the comparison is between model heads trained on PARDIG and IMERG targets. the research desk did not independently audit or reproduce these baselines.

brief.title: Google releases PARDIG global precipitation datasets with author-reported multi-network evaluation
brief.why_it_matters: A licensed global precipitation record at 15-minute cadence and roughly 10 km grid spacing can support weather, hydrology and climate research, especially where ground measurements are sparse. If the reported comparisons hold, its spaceborne-radar training and dense outputs may improve precipitation analysis and downstream forecasting. The evidence remains a first-party paper and data release, with regional coverage limits and important polar, mountain and early-record caveats.

related.summary: The WeatherNext 3 development predates the PARDIG public release and reports precipitation-head evaluations; the PARDIG paper says a closely similar earlier PARDIG version was used as a training target and reports improved early-lead precipitation forecasts. Both performance accounts remain first-party.

other.title: WeatherNext 3 moves operational global AI forecasting toward raw observations, hourly refresh and high-resolution probabilistic outputs
other.summary: Google Research and Google DeepMind report and operate WeatherNext 3, a global probabilistic weather model that augments conventional atmospheric analyses with low-latency geostationary satellite observations, produces a new forecast every hour, predicts single-level variables at hourly 0.1-degree resolution, and directly models observation-derived precipitation, sparse station measurements and cyclone attributes. In year-long 2024 evaluations it beats WeatherNext 2 on all tested surface variables and most upper-level analysis targets, while observation-based heads show large short-lead improvements against held-out stations and multiple precipitation ground truths. A six-week quasi-real-time 2026 comparison reports roughly 10% average first-week upper-level CRPS improvement versus ECMWF AIFS ENS v2. The advance is operationally meaningful because it begins collapsing data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing into a single learned system that can exploit observations newer than the latest global analysis state. The paper also documents important limits: some baseline/ground-truth mismatches, small real-time sample duration, under-spread cyclone ensembles, mesh artifacts and temporal discontinuities, no extreme-precipitation validation, and one poorly performing output withheld from operations.
